title: Jardiance and Alcohol: Ketoacidosis Risk, Dehydration and Safe Limits
excerpt: Can you drink alcohol on Jardiance (empagliflozin)? How heavy drinking raises the risk of ketoacidosis and dehydration, what moderate means, and the warning signs that need care.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Jardiance? How alcohol raises ketoacidosis and dehydration risk with empagliflozin, safe limits, and warning signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Jardiance (empagliflozin) has no direct chemical clash with alcohol the way some drugs do, and many people who take it can have an occasional drink if their doctor agrees. The real concern is a rare but serious side effect called **ketoacidosis**, a dangerous build-up of acids in the blood. Drinking too much alcohol is one of the risk factors listed on Jardiance's own US prescribing label, and with this class of drug ketoacidosis can happen even when your blood sugar looks normal. Heavy drinking also adds to the fluid loss Jardiance already causes, which can leave you dizzy and dehydrated. This guide explains how the two interact, what "moderate" means in practice, and the warning signs that mean you should get help right away.

**The quick rules:** Ask your doctor whether alcohol is OK for you specifically. If your doctor says drinking is OK, let them set the amount, never binge, eat a proper meal, and drink water alongside. Don't drink heavily while fasting, on a very low-carb or keto diet, or when you're sick. If you're vomiting and can't keep food or fluids down after drinking, call your doctor or care team, because that's when Jardiance can become risky. If you feel very sick, have stomach pain, or are breathing fast or hard, get emergency care and tell them you take Jardiance.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the official prescribing information. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, and you should not stop or change your Jardiance dose on your own. **Talk to your doctor before drinking alcohol on Jardiance**, especially if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, have heart failure or kidney disease, follow a low-carb diet, or drink more than a couple of drinks at a time. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you have nausea or vomiting that won't stop, stomach pain, unusual tiredness or weakness, trouble breathing or fast deep breathing, or confusion, even if your blood sugar reading is normal.

## What Jardiance Does in Your Body

Jardiance is the brand name for **empagliflozin**. It belongs to a group of medicines called **SGLT2 inhibitors**, sometimes nicknamed "gliflozins." It was first approved in the US for type 2 diabetes and is now also prescribed to lower the risk of heart and kidney problems in people with heart failure and chronic kidney disease, including some people who don't have diabetes at all.

Here's the mechanism in plain words. Your kidneys filter sugar out of your blood all day, then pull almost all of it back in so you don't lose it. A transporter protein called **SGLT2**, which sits in the tubes of the kidney, does most of that pulling back. Jardiance blocks it. So instead of being reabsorbed, a chunk of that sugar leaves your body in your urine.

That one action has several knock-on effects that matter when you drink:

- **You pee out more water.** Sugar in the urine drags water with it, so people on Jardiance urinate more and lose a little more fluid than usual.
- **Your body shifts toward burning fat.** Losing sugar in the urine nudges your metabolism toward using fat for fuel, which produces substances called **ketones**. In most people this stays at a harmless, low level.
- **Insulin levels tend to drift down a bit, and glucagon (the hormone that raises blood sugar) up a bit.** That hormone balance is part of why ketones rise.
- **Blood sugar falls without forcing your pancreas to make more insulin.** That's why Jardiance on its own rarely causes low blood sugar.

Alcohol touches almost every one of those same systems, which is why the combination deserves some thought even though it isn't a classic drug-to-drug interaction.

## Jardiance and Alcohol: The Ketoacidosis Risk

This is the most important section of this page.

### What ketoacidosis is

**Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)** happens when the body doesn't have enough insulin to use sugar for fuel, so it breaks down fat very fast and floods the blood with ketones. Ketones are acidic. When they build up faster than the body can clear them, the blood becomes too acidic, and that's a medical emergency that usually needs hospital treatment.

### Why SGLT2 inhibitors make it trickier

In 2015 the FDA issued a safety warning that SGLT2 inhibitors, including empagliflozin, can lead to ketoacidosis, and the warning now appears on the Jardiance label. The cases are uncommon, but there's a twist that makes them dangerous: with these medicines, ketoacidosis can occur when blood sugar is **normal or only mildly raised**. Doctors call this **euglycemic DKA** ("euglycemic" means normal blood sugar).

That's a problem because most people with diabetes are taught to watch for very high sugar readings as the warning sign. On Jardiance, the drug keeps pushing sugar out in the urine, so your glucose meter can look reassuring while ketones quietly climb. People and even emergency staff can miss it if they don't know you take an SGLT2 inhibitor.

### Where alcohol comes in

The Jardiance prescribing information lists factors that make ketoacidosis more likely. These include a sudden drop in food intake or calorie restriction, acute illness, surgery, a reduction in insulin dose, problems with the pancreas making insulin, and **alcohol abuse**. The patient medication guide puts it in everyday language as drinking too much alcohol.

There are a few reasons heavy drinking pushes in the wrong direction:

1. **Alcohol is processed in a way that favors ketone production.** When your liver breaks down a lot of alcohol, it changes the chemical balance inside liver cells. That shift slows the liver's ability to make new glucose and makes it easier to churn out ketones. In fact, heavy drinking on its own, with no medication involved, can cause a related condition called **alcoholic ketoacidosis**.
2. **Heavy drinking often comes with not eating.** Skipping dinner, drinking instead of eating, or not being able to face food the next day all cut your carbohydrate intake. Low food intake is a separate risk factor on the label.
3. **Vomiting and dehydration compound it.** A bad night that ends in vomiting means lost fluid, no food staying down, and stress hormones that raise ketones further.

Put together, a binge, an empty stomach, and a morning of vomiting is close to the textbook setup for ketoacidosis in someone taking an SGLT2 inhibitor. One glass of wine with a meal is a very different situation.

### Signs of ketoacidosis to know

The Jardiance label tells patients to stop taking it and get medical help right away if they have symptoms of ketoacidosis. These include:

- Nausea or vomiting
- Pain in the stomach area
- Unusual tiredness or weakness
- Trouble breathing, or fast, deep breathing
- Feeling confused or very sleepy
- A fruity smell on the breath (not listed on every label, but a classic sign of high ketones)

Notice the overlap with a hangover. Nausea, vomiting, tiredness, and a sore stomach are exactly what a rough morning after feels like. That's the trap. If you're on Jardiance and your "hangover" is unusually bad, isn't improving with water and food, or comes with heavy or fast breathing, don't wait it out. Seek care and tell them you take an SGLT2 inhibitor so they check your ketones and blood acid levels, not just your sugar.

## Jardiance, Alcohol, and Dehydration

Both Jardiance and alcohol make you lose fluid, through different routes.

- **Jardiance** pulls water out with the sugar it sends into your urine. The label warns that it can cause **volume depletion**, meaning low body fluid, which can show up as dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling faint, especially when you stand up. This is more likely in older adults, people with kidney problems, people with low blood pressure, and people taking diuretics (water pills).
- **Alcohol** blocks a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. With less of it, you pee more. That's why you're up at night after drinking and why you wake up thirsty. We cover this in more detail in [does alcohol dehydrate you?](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you)

Stack the two and the fluid losses add up. Practical effects can include:

- Feeling dizzy or lightheaded when you stand
- A worse headache and dry mouth the next morning
- Lower blood pressure than usual
- Extra strain on the kidneys when you're already dry

Dehydration also feeds back into the ketoacidosis risk, because a dried-out body is less able to clear ketones. The fix is simple but worth doing on purpose: drink water between alcoholic drinks and before bed, and keep drinking fluids the next day. If you have heart failure and your doctor has given you a fluid limit, follow their numbers rather than general hydration advice.

## Jardiance, Alcohol, and Low Blood Sugar

On its own, Jardiance rarely causes low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), because it doesn't force your pancreas to release insulin. That changes when you combine it with other diabetes medicines.

Alcohol lowers blood sugar in its own way. While your liver is busy breaking down alcohol, it's slower to release stored glucose and make new glucose. That effect can last for hours, including overnight and into the next morning, which is why drinking-related lows often happen while people are asleep.

The risk of a low is higher if you take Jardiance together with:

- **Insulin**
- **Sulfonylureas**, such as glipizide, glyburide, or glimepiride

The Jardiance label itself notes that the risk of low blood sugar goes up when it's used with insulin or insulin secretagogues (drugs like sulfonylureas that push the pancreas to release insulin), and that lower doses of those medicines may be needed. Add alcohol, especially on an empty stomach, and the odds of a low go up further.

If you're in that group:

- Eat food that contains carbohydrates while you drink.
- Check your blood sugar before bed and consider a snack if it's on the low side.
- Make sure the people you're with know you have diabetes, because a low can look a lot like being drunk.
- Ask your doctor whether you should adjust anything on days you plan to drink.

Our guide to [alcohol and blood sugar management](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) goes deeper on how different drinks affect glucose. For how other common prescriptions interact with alcohol, see our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Can You Drink on Jardiance? What "Moderate" Means

There's no blanket rule that people on Jardiance must never drink. The prescribing information does not ban alcohol. It warns about excessive use. Whether any amount is right for you depends on your overall health, your other medicines, and how well your diabetes, heart, or kidney condition is controlled, which is why your doctor is the right person to ask.

For people with diabetes in general, the American Diabetes Association's standard advice is that adults who choose to drink should do so in moderation: no more than one drink a day for women and no more than two for men. A standard drink in the US is about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits. That's a general ceiling for people with diabetes, not a green light on Jardiance. Your own limit, if any, should come from the doctor who prescribes it, because it depends on your kidneys, your other medicines, and how well your blood sugar is controlled.

If your doctor is fine with occasional drinking, these habits keep the risks lower:

| Do | Avoid |
|---|---|
| Drink with a meal that includes some carbohydrates | Drinking on an empty stomach or instead of dinner |
| Alternate each drink with a glass of water | Binge drinking or "catching up" quickly |
| Choose lower-sugar options (dry wine, light beer, spirits with a zero-sugar mixer) | Sugary cocktails and large measures |
| Check your blood sugar if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea | Drinking when you're already sick, vomiting, or not eating |
| Have a plan to get home and someone who knows you take Jardiance | Heavy drinking while on a keto or very low-carb diet |

### A special warning for low-carb and keto diets

Many people with type 2 diabetes cut carbs, and that's often a sensible choice. But very low-carb or ketogenic diets already raise ketone levels, and that's an extra risk factor on top of Jardiance. Add a night of heavy drinking and you're stacking three things that all push toward ketoacidosis. If you follow a strict low-carb plan, talk to your doctor about it specifically, and be especially cautious with alcohol. Our article on [how alcohol affects ketosis](/never-hungover/alcohol-ketogenic-diet-ketosis-impact-analysis-2025) explains the overlap.

## How Long After Taking Jardiance Can You Drink?

People often ask whether they can just space out their pill and their drinks. Unfortunately, timing doesn't really help with this medicine.

Jardiance is taken once a day, and the label lists its half-life (the time it takes for the level in your blood to fall by half) at roughly 12 hours. Because you take it every day, there's always some in your system. Skipping a dose to "make room" for a night out isn't recommended unless your doctor tells you to, and it won't instantly reverse the drug's effects.

What matters much more than the clock is **how much** you drink, **whether you eat**, and **whether you're well**. A drink with dinner is a lower-risk situation at any time of day. A binge on an empty stomach is risky no matter when you took your pill.

## When to Pause Jardiance: Sick Days and Surgery

This is useful to know even if you rarely drink.

**Sick days.** Many diabetes care teams give people on SGLT2 inhibitors "sick-day rules." The general idea is to temporarily stop the medicine if you're unwell enough that you can't eat or drink normally, for example with vomiting, diarrhea, a fever, or dehydration, and to restart once you're eating and drinking again. A day of vomiting after a heavy night counts. Ask your doctor for your own written sick-day plan, because the details vary, especially if you also use insulin.

**Surgery and procedures.** The Jardiance label advises stopping it at least 3 days before scheduled surgery, because fasting and the stress of surgery raise the ketoacidosis risk. Your surgical team should tell you when to stop and restart. Fasting is part of the same risk picture that alcohol plays into.

**Never stop on your own for the long term.** Jardiance protects the heart and kidneys for many people. If alcohol and this medicine don't fit your life, have that conversation with your doctor rather than quietly dropping the pill.

## Synjardy, Glyxambi, and Trijardy: Combination Pills and Alcohol

Empagliflozin also comes combined with other diabetes drugs in a single tablet. If you take one of these, alcohol considerations from both ingredients apply.

- **Synjardy and Synjardy XR (empagliflozin plus metformin).** Metformin carries a boxed warning about a rare but serious condition called **lactic acidosis**, and its label warns that alcohol increases metformin's effect on lactate. The Synjardy label tells patients to avoid excessive alcohol intake. That means two separate acid-related risks (ketoacidosis from the empagliflozin and lactic acidosis from the metformin) both get worse with heavy drinking. Our guide to [metformin and alcohol](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol) covers the metformin side in detail.
- **Glyxambi (empagliflozin plus linagliptin).** Linagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor, which on its own has a low risk of low blood sugar. The main alcohol concerns here are the empagliflozin ones: ketoacidosis and dehydration.
- **Trijardy XR (empagliflozin, linagliptin, and metformin).** All of the above apply, including the metformin warning.

## Do Other SGLT2 Inhibitors Work the Same Way?

Yes. The ketoacidosis warning applies to the whole class, so the same advice holds for:

- **Farxiga** (dapagliflozin)
- **Invokana** (canagliflozin)
- **Steglatro** (ertugliflozin)
- **Inpefa** (sotagliflozin), which is approved for heart failure

The details on each label differ slightly, but the basic message is the same: excessive alcohol is a risk factor for ketoacidosis, and dehydration is a shared concern.

## Does Alcohol Make Jardiance Less Effective?

Alcohol doesn't stop Jardiance from blocking SGLT2 in your kidneys. But drinking can still work against what you're taking it for:

- **Sugary drinks add a lot of sugar and calories.** Cocktails, sweet wines, ciders, and regular sodas as mixers can raise blood sugar more than the drug can offset.
- **Alcohol adds calories with little nutrition**, which can undo some of the modest weight loss many people see on Jardiance.
- **Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure and strains the heart.** If you take Jardiance for heart failure, that's moving in the opposite direction from your treatment goals.
- **Heavy drinking is linked to fatty liver** and to worse diabetes control over time.

So the effect isn't on the pill itself. It's on your overall blood sugar, weight, heart, and liver, which are the reasons you're taking it.

## The Jardiance Hangover: Why the Morning After Can Feel Worse

People on Jardiance sometimes say their hangovers feel worse than they used to. That makes sense. You start the night slightly drier than someone not on the drug, alcohol adds more fluid loss, and the morning after you may be lower on both fluid and carbohydrates than usual.

To make the next day easier and safer:

- **Rehydrate early.** Water, and an electrolyte drink if you've been sweating or vomiting. Choose a low-sugar electrolyte option if you're watching your glucose.
- **Eat breakfast.** Don't skip food because you feel rough. Food helps steady your blood sugar and limits ketone build-up.
- **Check your blood sugar** if you use insulin or a sulfonylurea, and test for ketones if your care team has given you a meter or urine strips and you feel unwell.
- **Know where the line is.** A normal hangover gradually improves as the day goes on with fluids and food. If yours is getting worse, you can't keep anything down, or your breathing feels off, treat it as possible ketoacidosis and get help.

A note on ketone tests: if you have a blood ketone meter, use it rather than urine strips if you can, since blood readings are more up to date. Ask your doctor what levels should prompt a call or an emergency visit for you. Don't use your glucose reading alone to decide you're fine, because on Jardiance it can look normal during ketoacidosis.

## When to See a Doctor

**Call your doctor or care team soon if:**

- You've been vomiting, or you can't eat or drink normally, for more than a few hours
- You're regularly having more than a couple of drinks at a time and you're on Jardiance
- You feel dizzy or faint when standing, or your blood pressure is lower than usual
- You've had low blood sugar episodes after drinking

**Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if you have:**

- Nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain that's severe or getting worse
- Fast, deep, or labored breathing
- Confusion, extreme sleepiness, or trouble staying awake
- Unusual weakness or tiredness that's out of proportion to a normal hangover
- A low blood sugar you can't bring up, or someone with diabetes who is unresponsive

Tell the medical team you take Jardiance (empagliflozin), so they check ketones and blood acid levels even if your sugar is normal.

## Can a Supplement Help?

Some people who drink occasionally look at supplements to make the morning after easier. Here's an honest view, with the caveat that this matters much less than the basics above.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers the risk of ketoacidosis, dehydration, or low blood sugar on Jardiance, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe on this medicine. It also hasn't been studied in people taking SGLT2 inhibitors, so check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding it, as you would with any supplement. If you and your doctor decide it's reasonable for an occasional night out, a well-reviewed option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and the premium [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) adds other ingredients. Read the full label to check for added sugars or anything else your care team would want to know about. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers how DHM fits alongside common prescriptions, and the [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing.

The bigger wins are free: drink less, eat with your drinks, alternate with water, and know the warning signs. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- Jardiance doesn't react with alcohol directly, and the label doesn't ban drinking. It warns against **excessive** alcohol use.
- The main risk is **ketoacidosis**, which on Jardiance can happen with normal blood sugar. Heavy drinking, skipping food, vomiting, low-carb diets, and illness all raise that risk.
- Jardiance and alcohol both make you lose fluid, so **dehydration and dizziness** are more likely when you drink.
- **Low blood sugar** becomes a concern if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea.
- If you drink, keep it moderate, eat, hydrate, and avoid binges. If you're vomiting or can't eat, call your care team, and treat severe symptoms or abnormal breathing as an emergency.
- Ask your doctor what's safe for you, and don't stop Jardiance on your own.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Jardiance?**

Many people on Jardiance can have an occasional drink if their doctor agrees, because there's no direct chemical interaction and the label doesn't ban alcohol. It does warn that excessive alcohol use raises the risk of ketoacidosis, a serious build-up of acids in the blood. If your doctor says drinking is OK, eat a meal with it, drink water alongside, and avoid binges. Ask your doctor what's safe for you, especially if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea.

**Does alcohol increase the risk of ketoacidosis on Jardiance?**

Yes, heavy drinking does. The Jardiance prescribing information lists alcohol abuse as a factor that makes ketoacidosis more likely, alongside low food intake, acute illness, and surgery. Alcohol shifts the liver toward making ketones, and heavy drinking often comes with not eating and with vomiting, which add to the risk. With SGLT2 inhibitors, ketoacidosis can happen even when blood sugar looks normal, so don't rely on your glucose reading alone.

**What are the signs of ketoacidosis on Jardiance?**

Watch for nausea or vomiting, stomach pain, unusual tiredness or weakness, trouble breathing or fast deep breathing, confusion, and sometimes a fruity smell on the breath. These can look like a bad hangover, which is what makes them easy to miss. If symptoms are severe, getting worse, or include breathing changes, get emergency care and tell the team you take Jardiance so they check ketones, not just blood sugar.

**How long after taking Jardiance can I drink alcohol?**

Timing doesn't make much difference. Jardiance is taken once a day and has a half-life of roughly 12 hours, so some is always in your system. What matters more is how much you drink, whether you've eaten, and whether you're well. Don't skip doses to make room for drinking unless your doctor tells you to.

**Can Jardiance and alcohol cause dehydration?**

Yes. Jardiance sends sugar into your urine, which pulls water with it, and alcohol blocks the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Together they can leave you dehydrated, dizzy, or lightheaded, especially when standing up. Drink water between alcoholic drinks and the next morning, and follow your doctor's fluid limits if you have heart failure.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol on Synjardy?**

Synjardy combines empagliflozin with metformin, so both medicines' warnings apply. Heavy drinking raises the risk of ketoacidosis from the empagliflozin and of lactic acidosis from the metformin, and the label tells patients to avoid excessive alcohol. Occasional moderate drinking may be acceptable for some people, but ask your doctor first.

**Does alcohol cause low blood sugar with Jardiance?**

Jardiance alone rarely causes low blood sugar. The risk rises if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea such as glipizide or glimepiride, and alcohol adds to it by slowing the liver's release of glucose for hours, including overnight. If you take those medicines, eat while you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and ask your doctor whether to adjust anything on drinking days.

**Should I stop taking Jardiance if I plan to drink?**

Don't stop Jardiance on your own. For many people it protects the heart and kidneys as well as lowering blood sugar. Instead, ask your doctor whether moderate drinking is OK for you and what your sick-day rules are. Many care teams advise pausing SGLT2 inhibitors temporarily when you're vomiting or can't eat or drink normally, then restarting once you're well.
